contentHtml:
Synopsis

India’s market for dermatologist-recommended skincare and haircare products is projected to reach Rs 10,400 crore by 2030. Consumer interest in scientifically backed solutions is increasing, although access and affordability are challenges. The report suggests that many consumers still self-medicate or rely on over-the-counter products without consulting dermatologists. Online channels are expected to grow significantly, while traditional outlets will face slower growth.

Listen to this article in summarized format

India’s market for dermatologist-recommended skincare and haircare products is expected to nearly double to Rs 10,400 crore by 2030, as consumers increasingly seek clinically backed solutions, although affordability and limited access to dermatologists remain key barriers to wider adoption, according to a report by research firm 1Lattice.

The market, estimated at Rs 5,900 crore in 2025, is projected to grow at an annual rate of about 12%, faster than the broader skincare and haircare market, which is expected to expand at around 10% to Rs 1.16 lakh crore over the same period.

Consumer interest in scientific validation is high: 90% of respondents said they preferred scientific or clinical proof over brand storytelling, while 86% said natural or organic claims alone were no longer sufficient. Yet awareness of clinical testing remains limited, with 45% saying they had never heard of clinical or in-vivo testing.

The survey also points to a gap between interest in dermatological care and actual access. Nearly half consulted a dermatologist first when faced with a skin or hair concern, while the rest initially relied on over-the-counter products, self-medication, online searches or other sources.

Among those who did not consult a dermatologist first, 38% cited the lack of an easily accessible dermatologist nearby and an equal proportion pointed to consultation costs. Access gaps were more pronounced outside metros.

“Indian consumers are asking for proof, but too many still have to figure out their skin concerns on their own. The next opportunity is not simply to sell more skincare. It is to make credible skin assessment, dermatologist-led guidance and effective products work together,” said Hitaysh Dhingraa, co-founder of Puresta.

Dr Chytra V Anand, managing director of dermatology and co-founder and chief formulator of Puresta, said consumers needed greater clarity on what works for their skin. “Clinical evidence and concern-led formulations matter, but so does knowing when to seek professional advice. Making that guidance easier to access can improve how people choose and use skincare,” she said.

The report estimates the broader cosmeceuticals market at Rs 14,400 crore in 2025, with a projected value of Rs 24,300 crore by 2030. It cautions that these categories overlap, as some brands operate across conventional skincare and clinically positioned products.

Online channels are expected to grow at around 23% annually through 2030, compared with 6% for offline channels, taking their share of the broader skincare and haircare market to 35% from 20% in 2025, according to 1Lattice estimates.

Ashish Dhir, senior director, consumer and retail at 1Lattice, said the growing interest in clinically backed products beyond metros offered significant headroom for category expansion.

However, the report flags affordability, distribution economics and the need to establish clinical credibility as key challenges. It also notes that dermatologist access and professional advocacy remain important constraints for brands seeking to expand beyond urban markets.

Global brands such as Cetaphil, Bioderma and CeraVe compete with domestic players including Fixderma, Minimalist and The Derma Co. Large consumer goods companies have also entered the segment, with Hindustan Unilever acquiring a 90.5% stake in Minimalist in 2025, while Honasa Consumer owns The Derma Co.
